questions.prompt: Peterson's opening claim about life-vision is best summarized as:
choices: A Vision is optional if you follow trends.
B There is no no-vision option—only better/worse visions (or someone else's).
C Only governments supply personal visions.
D Hedonism eliminates the need for vision.
questions.explain: You will be governed by a vision—good, bad, or borrowed.

questions.prompt: A plan, relative to a vision, is:
choices: A Broader and less actionable.
B A narrowed, focused vision aimed at implementation.
C A rejection of all theory.
D Identical to chaos.
questions.explain: Vision is broad theory; plan focuses it to an implementable point.

questions.prompt: Chaos, in his experiential map, includes:
choices: A Only political disorder.
B What you don't understand—and thus potential for new knowledge.
C Only moral evil.
D The domain where actions always succeed.
questions.explain: Unknown territory is chaos and also potential.

questions.prompt: Interest/grip when you're at the edge of knowledge is described as:
choices: A bug to eliminate with boredom.
B A manifestation of the learning instinct / meaning signal.
C Proof that security alone is enough.
D Evidence you should never leave home.
questions.explain: Interest grips you at the edge of what you know—optimized learning.

questions.prompt: Pure security without transformation is problematic because:
choices: A It maximizes adventure automatically.
B It lacks the transformative element needed to move toward a better self/world.
C It guarantees Pareto success.
D It is identical to meaning.
questions.explain: Security alone has no transformation; you also need the developmental edge.

questions.prompt: Pareto-style progress in accomplishment, as he uses it, suggests:
choices: A Progress is strictly linear and slow forever.
B Success compounds—early gains make later gains easier (geometric/exponential flavor).
C Only lottery winners improve.
D First albums are always easiest.
questions.explain: Success builds on itself across domains—start even if slow.

questions.prompt: On asking for a raise, he emphasizes:
choices: A Never documenting contributions.
B Presenting a real story of how you made the employer's life easier/more profitable.
C Threatening without alternatives.
D Working invisibly forever.
questions.explain: People need to know you're doing a good job—bring a concrete list when seeking promotion.

questions.prompt: The knight's darkest forest entry point symbolizes:
choices: A Avoiding all fear indefinitely.
B Entering chaos/potential at the frightening place that is yours to confront.
C Following only public maps.
D Waiting for guaranteed outcomes.
questions.explain: Enter where it looks darkest to you—same destination via fearful entry points.

questions.prompt: Therapy's truth-telling and story-straightening is framed as:
choices: A Entertainment only.
B Exposure to the unknown—clarifying past/present/future vision.
C A way to avoid responsibility.
D Proof trauma never matters.
questions.explain: Getting the story straight is therapeutic exposure and vision work.

questions.prompt: Voluntarily confronting small obstacles has what advantage?
choices: A It only shrinks fear of that one object.
B You simultaneously confront the broader domain of fear and become braver.
C It makes all relationships worse forever.
D It replaces bravery with numbness.
questions.explain: Small voluntary confrontations generalize—building bravery.

questions.prompt: Letting kids suffer appropriately is justified so that you don't:
choices: A Teach them sports.
B Steal their destinies by doing everything for them.
C Ever discipline them.
D Allow any play.
questions.explain: Mothers must let kids suffer some so destinies aren't stolen.

questions.prompt: Hobbes vs Rousseau, as he sketches walls/order:
choices: A Hobbes sees natural state as chaos/malevolence needing restraint; Rousseau sees restraints as corrupting intrinsic goodness.
B Both deny any human conflict.
C Rousseau invented prisons; Hobbes invented play.
D They agree people need no walls.
questions.explain: Hobbes: nasty/brutish/short natural state; Rousseau: intrinsic goodness corrupted by strictures.

questions.prompt: Constrained choice (e.g., two outfits) helps because:
choices: A Infinite options always maximize happiness.
B Walling off options reduces paralysis amid too many alternatives.
C Children should never choose.
D Consumer research forbids limited shelves.
questions.explain: Constrained choice (and consumer literature on too many shampoos) shows limits can help.

questions.prompt: Invitation over compulsion in partnerships/business means:
choices: A Manipulate first, apologize later.
B Offer solutions seeking voluntary assent; force/deception blocks the shared destination.
C Never negotiate dishes or chores.
D Always win by lowering the other.
questions.explain: Compulsion/deception instead of voluntary assent prevents reaching goals.

questions.prompt: Motivations/emotions help you by:
choices: A Removing all categorization of the world.
B Providing basic structures that help categorize experience and set goals.
C Eliminating the need for senses.
D Guaranteeing no conflicts ever.
questions.explain: Motivations and emotions structure understanding alongside sensory framing.

questions.prompt: Socialization is less 'forceful suppression' and more:
choices: A Deleting anger permanently.
B Offering better games that integrate aggression/needs into playable, long-term patterns.
C Ignoring toilet training.
D Keeping children as pure id.
questions.explain: You're offering a better game—e.g., sit until you can play civilly again.

questions.prompt: Conscience, in his account, is notable because:
choices: A You can shut it off at will if it were merely 'you'.
B It has autonomy—it calls you to account, pointing toward who you could become.
C It only praises you.
D It is identical to Twitter.
questions.explain: If conscience were fully you, you could silence it; its autonomy points to higher unity.

questions.prompt: The world shows up primarily as:
choices: A list of inert objects plus optional values painted on later.
B Pathways, tools, and obstacles (with most of reality invisible).
C Only mathematical equations.
D Random noise without goals.
questions.explain: You don't see bare objects then add value—world appears as pathways/tools/obstacles.

questions.prompt: If you don't know what to do, 'nothing' is:
choices: A The optimal moral solution.
B The wrong solution—better to try games others play than no game.
C Required by nihilism forever.
D Only for infants.
questions.explain: No game means no progress; look at what others do and try.

questions.prompt: Breaking 'make dinner' into knife-to-table steps illustrates:
choices: A That abstract commands always suffice for toddlers.
B Decomposing identity/skills to implementable subroutines at the right level.
C That dinner is unimportant.
D That children should never help.
questions.explain: Train by finding the insufficiency level and building subroutines upward.

questions.prompt: Meaning, at the close of lecture 3, is:
choices: A purely abstract metaphysical luxury.
B The instinct signaling you're integrating motivations into improving multi-person games.
C Only a chemical accident with no use.
D Identical to fame.
questions.explain: Meaning tells you you're integrating lower systems into broader, repeating, improving games.

questions.prompt: Gray's Neuropsychology of Anxiety is praised for linking:
choices: A Only astrology and personality.
B Emotional response with brain anatomy and pharmacology.
C Diet fads to IQ.
D Music theory to taxes.
questions.explain: Gray connects emotion to anatomical and pharmacological brain function.

questions.prompt: Work, in sacrificial terms he connects to motivation, involves:
choices: A Avoiding all deferred gratification.
B Giving up present comfort to move toward valued future outcomes (sacrificial stance).
C Only unpaid volunteering.
D Never tracking goals.
questions.explain: Work exemplifies sacrificial relation—foregoing now for valued later ends.

questions.prompt: Self-authoring / vision programs are discussed as potentially costly because:
choices: A Cost always proves a scam.
B Paying seriously can signal commitment so you take the plan seriously.
C Free advice is always followed better.
D Vision cannot be written.
questions.explain: He notes people may pay a lot partly to take the vision exercise seriously.

questions.prompt: Hillsdale's low dropout is contrasted with typical ~50% rates to suggest:
choices: A Dropping out is always optimal.
B Institutions can run things so students finish—high dropout is inexcusable.
C Only conservative colleges teach math.
D Mystery means nothing can change.
questions.explain: A 1% dropout shows proper structure vs inexcusable mass dropout.

questions.prompt: Pathological daydreams (even murderous) can emerge when:
choices: A You always tell the truth.
B Problem-solving fantasy is suppressed/lied about long enough.
C You finish exposure therapy.
D You sleep eight hours.
questions.explain: Suppressed problem-solving can turn fantasy pathological—including violent themes.

questions.prompt: Those who insist they would never obey a totalitarian are, he warns:
choices: A Statistically the safest group.
B Often the most likely to comply—blindness to one's capacity is the risk.
C Immune by IQ alone.
D Exempt if they watch documentaries.
questions.explain: People who think themselves least likely may be most likely—assume it could be you.

questions.prompt: Job's ordeal is framed as archetypal because:
choices: A Only kings suffer.
B Everyone must contend with unjust suffering—possibly via children if not oneself.
C Tragedy is rare and ignorable.
D Satan never appears in literature.
questions.explain: Unjust suffering is universal; the story sits at culture's base.

questions.prompt: Ordinary Men's policemen become perpetrators how?
choices: A Overnight, with no steps.
B Incrementally—one bloody step at a time—until some even enjoy it.
C Only under alien mind control.
D Because they were all lifelong criminals.
questions.explain: Gradual compliance transforms ordinary men into worst murderers.

questions.prompt: Integrating the shadow / knowing you can be dangerous yields:
choices: A Uncontrolled cruelty as the goal.
B Formidableness—dangerousness integrated rather than naive helplessness.
C Permanent guilt with no action.
D Denial that evil exists.
questions.explain: Knowing you can be dangerous lets you integrate it and become formidable.

questions.prompt: Cain's second-rate sacrifices connect to pride because:
choices: A Pride always increases offering quality.
B Cutting corners assumes reality/God is too blind to notice—an arrogant gamble.
C Abel forbids all work.
D Sacrifice is only taxation.
questions.explain: Pulling wool over the father's eyes is arrogance; twisting reality snaps back.

questions.prompt: Abraham leaving comfort illustrates:
choices: A Satiation at home is the highest aim.
B Calling beyond mere satisfaction—risking adventure that founds a people.
C That Islam alone matters.
D That travel posters define destiny.
questions.explain: Abraham has satiation yet is called out—pattern of adaptation beyond comfort.

questions.prompt: Marriage shifts the center of gravity because:
choices: A It remains only about you.
B It's not about you anymore—harmony with spouse stabilizes the household and your psyche.
C Children forbid all games.
D Turn-taking is optional after age four.
questions.explain: Marriage demands sacrifice of pure self-focus; household sanity enables life.

questions.prompt: If someone lacks relationships, friends, and meaningful engagement, Peterson may say:
choices: A They definitely have major depression only.
B They may simply not have a life—a serious problem distinct from immunological depression.
C Cats fix everything.
D Cynicism proves enlightenment.
questions.explain: Multidimensional life assessment separates 'no life' misery from depression.

questions.prompt: Aiming fantasies at becoming attractive to a worthy partner is preferred over:
choices: A Any self-improvement.
B Waiting for someone whose life goal is to be 'right for you' as you are.
C Honesty about desires.
D Wanting children thoughtfully.
questions.explain: Better to become worthy of the person you'd want than demand they fit your unworked self.

questions.prompt: Surround yourself with people who:
choices: A Punish your small steps forward.
B Are aiming up—celebrate progress; don't cynically cut you down.
C Only gossip.
D Refuse all projects.
questions.explain: Aim-up companions matter; helping the willing differs from carrying the unwilling.

questions.prompt: A dead-end job, in his terms, often means:
choices: A Any job with a boss.
B A tyrannical ruler and no reward for good work—then look elsewhere.
C All employment is slavery.
D You must never leave.
questions.explain: Tyranny plus no reward for good work = reason to seek another place.

questions.prompt: The day confronts you as:
choices: A Fully determined with no possibility.
B An unformed realm of bounded possibility calling via conscience.
C Only a calendar app notification.
D Something to outsource entirely.
questions.explain: Each day is parameterized possibility that summons you.

questions.prompt: God's offer to Abraham (father of nations) is analogized to:
choices: A Personal brand sponsorships only.
B Establishing an adaptation pattern successful across generations—even via humble roles done well.
C Rejecting all family.
D Winning arguments online.
questions.explain: Cascading successful pattern down generations could be you—even as a devoted parent.

questions.prompt: A unserious vacation-poster 'vision' fails because:
choices: A Beaches are immoral.
B You must flesh out a realistic, serious vision of how much good you could do—not a teenage fantasy left unexamined.
C Canada forbids travel.
D Mai tais solve nihilism.
questions.explain: He mocks unexamined Caribbean-poster dreams; take yourself seriously and specify.
